name: Nora Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew of five at Midvale Energy, mostly on new connections: the cables that bring power into new housing estates, a solar farm, that kind of thing. Some days we're in a trench jointing underground cable, some days we're up poles running a new service. I do the paperwork too, and I check every joint before we backfill, because a bad joint is a fire in five years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money, mostly. Midvale pays less than the big city utilities, and my partner Marco is a self-employed plasterer, so his money comes in lumps. We're getting married next September and we had some saved, then his van's gearbox went in August, so we're back to almost nothing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. I'll read you five short pictures of the future and ask a few questions about each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I use AI now and then, mostly to tidy up my job notes, so I've seen what it can do and what it can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right to me. It's useful for tidying notes, and it doesn't dig trenches. I'd probably say that to the crew over lunch and not bother posting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the job's fine and the money's still tight. Midvale has a steady list of new estates for the next few years, so I'm not worried about work. I'm worried about paying for a wedding on a plasterer's lumpy income with less than a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and take the Saturday overtime on the solar farm connection, which pays time and a half. Marco and I would cut the wedding from a hundred and twenty guests to sixty, which we've been arguing about anyway. And I'd open a separate wedding account so the van can't eat it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not about AI. Just the normal tightness, like a harness that's a notch too snug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting the guests in half. How did that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It hasn't, yet. Marco wants everyone from his football team, and I want my aunts. A wedding for sixty means somebody's cousin isn't invited, and that's a fight I'd rather have than a debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What matters most to you at work right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew getting home safe. One of my lads, Tariq, is new and rushes the jointing. I'd rather check his work twice than have a cable fail in somebody's front garden in a few years' time.

say: AI is useful for tidying **notes**, and it doesn't dig trenches.
I'd say so to my **crew over lunch** and not bother posting it.
think: The job's fine, with a steady list of **new estates** ahead.
Paying for a **wedding** on lumpy income with under a month saved is the worry.
do: Take **Saturday overtime** on the solar farm connection at time and a half.
Cut the wedding from **120 guests to 60**.
Open a separate **wedding account** so the van can't eat it.
feel: **Uneasy**, but only the normal **tightness** of money, not AI.
S0.quote: A wedding for sixty means somebody's cousin isn't invited, and that's a fight I'd rather have than a debt.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money**, not work: a wedding and a partner's irregular income.
She's proud of **checking joints**, thinking years ahead about faults.
She'd rather have a **guest-list fight** than take on debt.

steps.text: Work Saturday overtime on the solar farm connection
Open a separate account for the wedding money
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 60

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is good for us, at least for a while. All those data centres running AI need power, and somebody has to connect them. I'd tell the crew we're about to be busier than we've ever been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the best of the five for me. The planning and paperwork side will change, sure, and maybe the design office shrinks. But Midvale would be begging for cable crews, and overtime is how Marco and I finally get a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift for the first year and put half of it straight into savings. I'd learn whatever new planning app they bring in, once a couple of other crew leads have tried it and it's not full of bugs. And I'd ask for a pay review, because if they need crews that badly, they can pay us like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit hopeful. For once the change seems to run my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the design office might shrink. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a bit. Lucy in design sends me cable drawings, and she's good, and she has two little ones. I'd hate to see her go, but I can't pretend my crew isn't safer than her desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a catch you can see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots, eventually. If machines can dig trenches and lay cable, my crew of five becomes a crew of two. But you said slowly, and slowly in our company means about ten years.

say: This one is good for us, because **data centres** need power.
We're about to be **busier** than we've ever been.
think: It's the **best of the five** for me, at least for a while.
**Overtime** is how my partner and I finally get a cushion.
do: Take every **overtime** shift in the first year and save half.
Learn the new **planning app** once other crew leads have tested it.
Ask for a **pay review** while crews are in demand.
feel: **Calm**, even **hopeful**, because the change runs my way for once.
S1.quote: All those data centres running AI need power, and somebody has to connect them.
fieldNote: She sees AI driving **grid demand**, which makes her crew more valuable.

Her one long-term fear is **trenching robots** shrinking her crew.

steps.text: Work every overtime shift in the first year
Put half of all overtime pay into savings
Learn the new planning app once other crew leads have tested it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow this down, and I don't usually say that about anything. Nobody's ready: not the company, not the government, not my family. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think both of us are in trouble, not just me. By 2028 the planning and paperwork part of my job is gone, and by 2031 a robot can joint cable, and Marco's plastering goes too. We'd be thirty-two with two hands-on trades and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd swap the big wedding for a small one at the registry office and put the deposit back in the bank. I'd save every penny of overtime between now and 2031, because those three years are the last good ones. And I'd look for training as a high-voltage tester, the person who signs off new equipment as safe, because someone will have to check the robots' work for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when you open a joint and find it was done wrong and buried for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Marco about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marco we should still marry, just smaller and sooner, at the registry office with our parents. The party can wait for a better year. He'd sulk for a day and then agree, because he's sensible underneath the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said those three years are the last good ones. What makes them good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side's gone by then, but somebody still has to be in the trench. If the company can't hire enough hands, those three years might pay better than ever. I'd squeeze them dry.

say: We need to **slow this down**, and I don't usually say that.
Nobody is **ready**: not the company, the government or my family.
think: Both of us are in **trouble**, not just me.
By 2031 robots take my **cable jointing** and my partner's plastering.
do: Swap the big wedding for a **registry office** ceremony and bank the deposit.
Train as a **high-voltage tester** who checks equipment is safe.
feel: **Alarmed**, like finding a bad joint that's been buried for years.
S2.quote: We'd be thirty-two with two hands-on trades and no savings.
fieldNote: Her alarm comes from **both earners** working in hands-on trades hit by 2031.
She sees **2028 to 2031** as the last good earning years and would squeeze them.
She'd keep the **marriage** but drop the party.

steps.text: Hold a small registry office wedding and bank the deposit
Save every penny of overtime until 2031
Train as a high-voltage equipment tester

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and start planning. I'd tell my crew to pick up an extra qualification while the company still pays for training. That's practical, and practical is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still bad for us, but survivable. By 2031 my paperwork's gone, by 2034 the trench work, and Marco's trade too. Five years means we can save a bit, marry properly, and get one of us into something steadier first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the high-voltage testing course in the second year, once I'd seen whether the first people through it got jobs. We'd keep the wedding at sixty guests and put whatever the aunts give us into savings. And I'd push Marco to learn to fit solar panels or heat pumps, something with years of installs ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It's a hard climb, not a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until the second year to start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen courses come and go. In my first year, half the crew did a smart-meter course and the smart-meter work went to a contractor. I'd let someone else find out if it's worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco about solar panels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it nicely, over a takeaway, not as a lecture. He hates being told what to do. But I'd show him the prices, and he can do sums.

say: Five years is enough if people stop arguing and start **planning**.
Crew members should get an extra **qualification** while the company still pays.
think: It's still bad for us, but **survivable**.
Five years lets us save, marry properly and get one of us somewhere **steadier**.
do: Take the **high-voltage testing** course in year two, once graduates have jobs.
Keep a **sixty-guest** wedding and save the gift money.
Push my partner to learn **solar or heat pump** fitting.
feel: **Anxious**, but I can breathe: a hard climb, not a fall.
S3.quote: In my first year, half the crew did a smart-meter course and the smart-meter work went to a contractor.
fieldNote: A wasted **smart-meter course** taught her to let others go first.
Five years lets her keep the **wedding**, only smaller.
She'd steer her partner toward **installation work** with years of demand ahead.

steps.text: Take the high-voltage testing course in year two
Bank the wedding gift money from the aunts
Hold the wedding with sixty guests next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's not panic and let's not waste it. That's my line at work and with friends. It's sensible, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough that I'd mostly get on with life. The robots come around 2039, when I'm nearly forty. By then I'd want to be the one testing the equipment, not laying the cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and taking the overtime for the first few years. We'd have the full wedding next September, all hundred and twenty, and start saving for a house deposit after that. I'd do the testing course around 2030, when there's still plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the way you are when the forecast says rain next week. You pack a coat and get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A house, on thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not soon. But ten years of steady work and overtime is enough for a small deposit, if we're careful. We'd buy something with a garage for Marco's van and stop paying someone else's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of this one that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork side, in 2036. If an AI plans the jobs and signs off the drawings, I'd want to know who's responsible when something goes wrong. A machine can't stand in front of an inspector and explain a bad joint.

say: We've got a **decade**, so let's not panic and let's not waste it.
I'd say the same **sensible** thing at work and with friends, and mean it.
think: Ten years is enough that I'd mostly **get on with life**.
By **2039** I'd want to be testing the equipment, not laying cable.
do: Keep taking **overtime** for the first few years.
Have the **full wedding** next September, then save for a house deposit.
feel: **Uneasy**, like rain forecast next week: pack a coat and carry on.
S4.quote: A machine can't stand in front of an inspector and explain a bad joint.
fieldNote: With a decade, she brings back the **full wedding** and a house plan.
Her live worry is **responsibility** when AI signs off drawings.
She plans a move from laying cable to **testing** it before 2039.

steps.text: Keep taking overtime for the next few years
Hold the full 120-guest wedding next September
Save for a small house deposit after the wedding
Take the high-voltage testing course around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marco and I would both be in hands-on trades with nothing saved and the robots only three years behind. What would help is training that's paid for and comes with a job at the end, and some kind of support for couples where both trades go at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the grid itself. Whatever happens with AI, all of it runs on electricity, and somebody has to build that. I wish more people understood that the people in the trench are holding the whole thing up.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with AI, all of it runs on electricity, and somebody has to build that.
portrait: Nora Santos, 27, leads a **five-person cable crew** connecting new estates for an inland utility.
She's saving for a **wedding** with a plasterer partner whose income comes in lumps.
She uses AI now and then and waits for **proof** before taking new courses.
She is **calm** in Steady Disruption, where grid demand brings overtime, and alarmed at AGI by 2028.
Her plan across the AGI pictures is to move from laying cable to **testing** it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both household trades hit and nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** that comes with a job at the end.
Support for couples whose **two trades** go at once.
